02

What it costs
to leave it

Three consequences, all of them things you are already paying for whether or not the line item exists.

Speed to lead decides the deal

The response that arrives in sixty seconds and the one that arrives tomorrow are competing for a decision that has usually already been made.

Attribution stays guesswork

Without a clean path from source to contact record, you cannot tell which channel deserves more budget. So the budget goes where it went last year.

Your pipeline lies to you

Stages that do not reflect how deals actually move produce forecasts nobody trusts and reports nobody reads.

04

How we work it

Four steps, with the real deliverable named at each one. If a step does not produce something you can hold, it is not a step.

Step 01

Map what happens now

Every path a lead can take today, including the informal ones people invented to get around the system.

Deliverable — Current-state flow map

Step 02

Design the flows

What fires, when, to whom, and what a human still needs to do. Automation that hides a person is worse than none.

Deliverable — Workflow specification

Step 03

Build and connect

Forms, fields, tags, pipeline stages, sequences and the integrations between them.

Deliverable — Configured CRM + live workflows

Step 04

Test every path end to end

Contact created, correct tags, correct stage, correct sequence, correct attribution. Every path, before launch.

Deliverable — QA log + documentation

07

The objections you were about to raise

Most people do. The question is whether the stages match how your deals actually move and whether anything happens automatically. Half-used CRMs are the norm, not the exception.

Bad ones do. The fix is specificity — referencing what someone actually told you — not sending less. A generic email written by a human is still generic.

It can be phased. Speed-to-lead on one path is usually a week of work and the single highest-return change available to most businesses.
